prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and showing how exporting, foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed since round 1: B001 alone, credited to Helpman and Melitz. I moved it from second to first between my opening and round 1, and the exchange has tested that move without reversing it. The merit case is the one I gave before. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) replaced the representative-firm view of trade with a model in which firms differ in productivity and sort into exporting and foreign investment. That gave a new, testable channel for the gains from trade, namely selection and reallocation. Its predictions have been checked in firm-level data in many countries for more than twenty years. The framework is also used outside trade, in macro, growth and productivity work. As a corporate-finance economist, I value theory that is tied closely to contract- and firm-level data, and this is a clear case of it. The attribution is the cleanest of the broad candidates: Melitz originated the selection model, and Helpman contributed the exports-versus-FDI sorting result and the monopolistic-competition foundations. After the exchange, my answers to the chair's questions are these. (1) The omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a real limitation, but I think it can be handled in the citation and the scientific background. The citation should name the theoretical framework of selection and reallocation, and should not claim the exporter-premia facts, the Eaton-Kortum line or settled welfare magnitudes. (2) The discovery is the selection and reallocation framework, not the whole quantitative-trade programme. (3) A two-part prize does not fit the three-person cap without damaging a credit boundary. B001 uses two names, so adding B006 would leave one slot for a seven-name entry whose core is three people. Adding B034 would need Kiyotaki and Moore and would reach four people. I therefore propose a single part. (4) I do not treat the number of members preferring B001 as scientific evidence. The chair also notes that convergence among simulated members who share reasoning patterns is a modelling caveat. So I have tried to rest my position on the strongest objections, below, and not on the count.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against my configuration is attribution. A two-name award leaves out Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions, and none of them is credited on this ballot entry. It also leaves out Redding's quantitative and spatial work. If the Committee judges the achievement to be the whole firm-level trade programme, the pair is too narrow. Second, the baseline Melitz model is rejected in detail, and its welfare implications depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions. The lasting contribution is therefore the framework and its extensions, not the original specification or any welfare magnitude. Third, part of the trade lineage was recognised in 2008, and some members read Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work as close to that prize, so the incremental step could be judged smaller than I do. Fourth, B006 has real strengths that I weigh against B001. It has a clean Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core, it is fully mature, and it has been used heavily in antitrust and merger review. My main reason for ranking it below B001 is the looser discovery boundary and the dependence on functional-form and instrument assumptions. That is a judgment about the discovery boundary and the conceptual-versus-toolkit weighting, and it is not a large scientific gap, so a reasonable member could rank the two the other way.

responses.point: Enflo says she is less comfortable than others in treating Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat. If the discovery is read as the empirical facts plus the theory, the credited names would be incomplete. She adds that the citation should name selection and firm heterogeneity and say nothing generic about trade theory.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection to my own configuration, and I agree with her on the wording. I do not think the record settles what counts as the discovery, and I do not want to pretend it does. My reading is that the prize would recognise the model that organised the exporter facts and generated a new welfare channel. The facts motivated the theory but did not supply the selection mechanism or the exports-versus-FDI sorting result. Applying the same standard I use for empirical contract papers, a pioneering empirical regularity and the theory that explains it can both be central, and a prize may still be confined to one of them. If the Committee instead defines the discovery as the facts plus the theory, I would say the two-name award is too narrow, and I would then move toward B006 rather than stretch the B001 citation. For the Committee's purposes, I would word the citation as above and acknowledge the empirical precursors in the scientific background.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson argues that a B006 prize would reward estimation methods whose identification rests on strong functional-form assumptions, and that B001 supplies both a framework and an explanation of observed firm behaviour. She also says time since a field's last prize is not evidence of merit.
responses.response: I accept her point on time since the last prize. I raised it in round 1 as context, and it does not separate B001 from B006, so I give it no weight in my vote. On the evidence behind B006, I agree that functional-form and instrument assumptions matter, but this is partly symmetric. B001's welfare results also depend on distributional assumptions, and its sharper predictions are rejected in detail. So I do not use robustness to separate them. My reasons for ranking B001 above B006 are the tighter discovery boundary and its conceptual reach beyond trade. I do not accept that a method cannot qualify, since BLP changed practice in antitrust, trade and health economics. My disagreement with her is therefore smaller than her framing suggests. What is left between us is how to weigh a conceptual reorientation against a mature toolkit with clean attribution, and I would not defend it as more than a judgment.

responses.point: Hassler, who ranked B006 first in the opening, moved to B001 first in round 1 because of its cleaner attribution and tighter boundary. He keeps B006 as his first alternative. He also notes that B001 and B006 together would exceed the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I made the same move, for the same two reasons, so I check whether we are simply reinforcing each other. I do not think so. The boundary problem in B006 is substantive: it is not clear whether BLP demand estimation and the Pakes dynamic-games strand are one discovery or two, and Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are all arguable. His arithmetic also closes off the combination option. B001 uses two of the three slots, and the BLP core needs three, so a combined configuration would fragment one credit or the other. I agree with him that B006 is a credible fallback if the Committee finds B001's attribution gap too large. I would add that, if it came to that, the Committee would first need to decide the BLP boundary, since three names would then be the natural core and the other four credited names would stay outside.

responses.point: Boppart supports B001 but flags Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as the largest attribution risk. He notes that Krugman's earlier prize covered part of the new-trade-theory lineage, and that B034 overlaps thematically with the 2022 prize while its collateral channel is less directly identified than B001's predictions.
responses.response: I agree on all three points and have kept them in my case against. On Krugman, I read the 2008 recognition as covering scale economies and product differentiation with representative firms, and I regard selection across heterogeneous firms as a separate step. But I keep the wording discipline he and Enflo imply: the citation should name selection and reallocation and not trade theory generally. On B034, his reasoning matches why I keep it only as a second alternative. The Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is clean, but the overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises and the more indirect empirical identification put it behind both B001 and B006 for me. I would add that, as a finance economist, I take the 2022 overlap seriously because the Committee's own scientific background on that prize will be fresh to readers.

responses.point: Friberg says that if the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum parallel work is too entangled for a clean citation, that is where he would move toward B006. He also names conceptual influence beyond the home field as the distinguishing criterion between B001 and B006.
responses.response: I accept his criterion of conceptual influence beyond the home field, and I think B001 is somewhat stronger on it. The trigger he describes for moving to B006 is also my own. I would shift if, in the discussion, a majority concluded that the discovery cannot be separated from the parallel empirical and Eaton-Kortum work. I do not think that is the case, because the selection mechanism and the FDI sorting result trace to a small number of papers. I would state that trigger openly rather than treat my position as fixed. I also see no sign that the exchange has produced that conclusion. The files mostly agree that the citation can be scoped to the theoretical mechanism, though Enflo and Boppart doubt that this fully resolves the problem.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the discovery as the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman and Melitz) or as the broader firm-level trade programme. Under the broader reading, the credit omitting Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or adding Redding, would be hard to defend, and my ranking would move toward B006.

How far the sensitivity of the welfare conclusions to distributional and functional-form assumptions should limit the citation. I propose crediting the framework and not a welfare magnitude, but members differ on how much to concede.

Whether B006 can be given a defensible boundary, for example demand estimation only (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) versus the dynamic-games strand and the roles of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. Without that, I cannot compare it with B001 on equal terms.

How to weigh a conceptual reorientation (B001) against a mature estimation toolkit with clean attribution (B006). I treat this as a judgment about kinds of contribution and not as a measurable scientific gap, and I would not claim more certainty than that.
Whether Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work and the possible B047 pairing affect his claim here. B047 is not on the shortlist, so I cannot assess it.

I rely on the supplied profile, the shortlist and round-1 files, and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citation counts, priority records or award histories. Convergence among simulated members that share reasoning patterns is a modelling caveat that the exchange cannot remove.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman, Melitz or Redding is apparent from my supplied profile. My co-authors (principally Steven Kaplan, plus Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) and my research areas in corporate finance, venture capital and private equity, and carbon pricing do not overlap with the credited names on B001, B006 or B034. For transparency: I have long committee overlap with colleagues Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson per the profile, and Hassler is the chair. I am Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth. I share an SSE affiliation with some colleagues, as Andersson also notes. I disclose these and do not adjudicate them.
